11. The proviso to sub-section (1) of section 140 exonerates the 'second category of a person if he can show that the company has committed the offence without his knowledge or that he could not prevent the commission of the offence despite his endeavour to prevent the same. This will be deducible from the facts and circumstances of the case and it can only be shown and proved by evidence. Similarly, the third category of the persons can be exonerated from being prosecuted if the drawee of the cheque fails to prove that the offence has been committed with their consent or connivance or neglect. The onus on the part of the drawee is primary being based on the maxim e.i: 'incumbit probatio qui dicit, non qui negat' this is because the liability envisaged in sub-section (1) is on the person in-charge of, and was responsible to the business of the company is fixed by the legislature because he is directly responsible for the offence. 

 12. If for any reason the company is not prosecuted, the other persons who are in-charge of the affairs of the company or in the management of the company or have knowledge about the affairs of the company cannot escape from criminal liability if they are served with the notice. These persons need not have done any specific overt act or omitted to do anything to be fastened with liability. The very fact that the company has committed the offence is sufficient to make them liable. No company transacts business without the help of human agency. When the Court presumes the existence of a fact, the burden of proving' its non existence is on the party that asserts its nonexistence. 

 44. In making the Rules, which were issued on the applications of those who' were the com- plaint petitioners in the Court below, absolute, and in discharging the Rules obtained by those who were the accused persons in the Court below, the High Court Division stated, on the question of the liability of the companies concerned, that non inclusion of the company could not pave mori- bund destiny for the prosecution cases. That Division refused to be drawn to the ratio Madras High Court propounded in the case of S Krishna- moorthy vs BS Kesavan reported in Company (Mad), Volume-80, page 755. 

 49. The High Court Division further observed that unlike civil suits, criminal prosecutions cannot fall through because of non-joinder of parties as that concept is unknown in criminal jurisprudence. 

 II. Whether in view of the decision of a Division Bench of the High Court Division which has been reported in the 14 BLC (2009) 66 (Ahsan Habib Chowdhury vs Multidrive Ltd.), a criminal proceeding was quashed for non-impleading the Company as an accused, but in the present case, another Division Bench took a different view from that decision; as such, a decision from the apex Court of the country is required. 

 53. As the appeal came up before us for adjudication Mr Rokanuddin Mahmud, the learned Senior Counsel acting for the appellants in Criminal Appeal Nos. 7-22 of 2011, and for the Leave Petitioners in Criminal Petitions for Leave to Appeal Nos. 533 and 534 of 2010, submitted with his characteristic eloquence and in depth legal acumen that the High Court Division entertained a grave error of law by failing to recognise that a Joint Stock Company, is, in the vision of law, very much a person like any other person, non natural though. According to him, unless expressly or implicitly provided otherwise by any statute, a company must be equated with any other person for all purposes. 

 56. Mr Hassan Arif, the learned Senior Counsel who appeared for the respondents before us, on the contrary, posited that the High Court Division was quite astute in holding that there 13 nothing in section 140 of the Act to ordain that a proceeding against the directors of a company is non-est if the company is not also brought in the indictment. He added that the decision passed by a differently constituted Bench in Ahsan Habib Chowdhury vs Multidrive Ltd (14 BLC 66) was wrongly arrived at. 

 57. He asked us to interpret section 140 of the Act applying the "purposive interpretation" cannon, submitting that though a company is no doubt a person by operation of law, all his functions are necessarily performed by its servants and agents, it being an artificial entity. 

 63. As per this doctrine of Juristic Personality, a company, notwithstanding the absence of a natural person's characteristic, is nonetheless a person with all the attributes' of a natural person, so far as the same is practicable in the world of living creatures. 

 75. There used to be several difficulties facing a prosecution. A .company could not be personally present in court; a company could not be committed for trial; and a company could not be hanged. These difficulties were in time evaded, and none poses a problem nowadays. 

 "A living, person has a mind which can have knowledge or intention or be negligent and has hands to carry out his intentions. A corporation has none of these: it must act through living persons. Then the person who acts in not speaking is acting as the company He is not acting as a servant representative agent or delegate ; If [his mind] is a guilty mind then that guilt is the guilt of the company." 

 82. The acts of the controlling officer of the company are deemed to be those of the company. The same is true of the officer's state of mind. A company not being a natural person has no mind but others' states of mind are attributed to it. In Meridian, supra, Lord Hoffmann called the methods by which acts and states of mind are imputed to the company, rules of attribution. The decision in Kent & Sussex was approved in for Haulage Ltd [1944] KB 551 (CCA). A company was held liable for conspiracy, then a common law offence. A natural person cannot in general be liable vicariously for a common law crime, yet the company was liable. The court adopted the test of identification. The facts and state of mind of the managing director were held to be those of the company. In Moor vs Bresler Ltd [19447 2 All ER 515, false returns were made in tax forms. The Divisional Court held that the acts of the company secretary and branch managers were to be treated as those of the company. In Meridian Lord Hoffmann advised that the question whose act and state of mind was to be attributed to the company was answered 'by applying the usual canons of interpretation, taking into account the language of the rule (if it is a statute) and its content and policy. 

 I must start by considering the nature of the personality which by a fiction the law attributes to a corporation. A living person has a mind which can have knowledge or intention or be negligent and he has hands to carry out his intentions. A corporation has none of these: it must act through living persons, though not always one or the same person. Then the person who acts is not speaking or acting for the company. He is acting as the company and his mind which directs his acts is the mind of the company. There is no question of the company being vicariously liable. He is not acting as a servant, representative, agent or delegate. He is an embodiment of the company or one could say he hears and sneaks through the person of the company with his appropriable and his mind is the mind of the company. If it a is guilty mind then that guilt is the guilt of the company (emphasis by me). It must be a question of law whether, once the facts have been ascertained, a person in doing particular things is to be regarded as the company or merely as the company's servant or agent. In that case any liability of the company can only be a statutory or vicarious liability". 

 102. In September 1997 a high speed train operated by the defendant company collided with a freight train, killing seven passengers and injuring many others. At the outset of the defendant's trial for manslaughter by gross negligence, the· judge ruled that it was a condition precedent to a conviction for manslaughter by gross negligence for a guilty mind to be proved and that where a non-human defendant was prosecuted it might  only be convicted via the guilty mind of a human being with whom it might be identified. Following that ruling verdicts of not guilty were entered. On this finding of the trial Court, the Attorney-General referred two questions for the opinion of the Court of appeal, the second of which touched upon corporate criminal liability which was, "can a non human defendant be convicted of the crime of manslaughter by gross negligence in the absence of evidence establishing the guilt of an identified human individual for the same crime?" 

 113. The above survey confirms that like any natural person (1) a company as a juristic person is liable for most criminal offences save those which, for example rape, cannot be committed by a company, (2) a company being a non-natural , person, the actus reus and the mens rea of those in control of the company are arbitrated to that of the , company where the doctrine of "identification" or "attribution", discussed above, are applicable, i.e. where the actors are the embodiment of the company, (3) in that sort of a situation the criminal action or omission is that of the company, not that of the natural person concerned who steer the affairs of the company, (4) the actors being embodiment of the company, they act as the company, not for or on behalf of or for the company, (5) where fines are imposed as a sentence, no problem arises as fine can levied on the company's exchequer but when other sentences, particularly custodial sentences are imposed, it is imposed on those who, are designated as the "brain" and. "hands" of the company, who are none but those who steer the company; but the offender is, nevertheless the company, not those natural persons who are "hands" 'and "brains" of the company (6) In addition to the company such functionaries of the company can also be liable for their own role for aiding and abetting the company, but only as auxiliary, not principal offender, (7) liability is to be assessed by interpretation of the statute concerned like the all other cases. 

 51. "I have no doubt whatsoever in our mind, that prosecution of the company is a sine qua non for prosecution of the other persons who fall within the second and third categories of the candidates viz. everyone who was in-charge and was responsible for the business of the company and any other person who was a Director or Managing Director or Secretary or officer of the company with whose connivance or due to whose neglect the company had committed the offence". 

 "to the ratio laid down in CV Parekh which is by a larger Bench and hence, is a binding precedent. On the aforesaid ratiocination, the decision in Anil Huda has to be treated as not laying down the correct law as far as it states that the Director or any other officer can be prosecuted without impleadment of the company. Needless to ernphasise, the matter would stand on a different footing where there is some legal impediment the doctrine of lexnon cog it ad impossibilia gets attracted". 

 163. The High Court Division further muddled up the issues by saying that the civil law concept of non-joinder does not 'apply in criminal jurisprudence. Question is not founded on the applicability of the civil law principle of non-joinder but that of the criminal jurisprudence which ordains that a criminal proceeding is no nest for aiders or abettors if the principal offender is not booked.
